Step one: Cracking your PSP

Disclaimer: I cannot take responsibility if you brick your PSP. It is a safe process if you follow the instructions, and I'm here to help if you need it.

Wololo's CFW for Dummies page. Just click which model you have and follow the instructions. It is an extremely easy process that only involves dropping files on your PSP and running them.

This is important: Do not update your PSP past 6.60 or this guide probably won't work. If you're below 6.60, there is a download link in the guide to get 6.60 and install it from a PC. There is no real advantage to upgrading to 6.61 other than being able to access the PSN store, and a bunch of plugins and extensions will break.

There are 'signed' emulators out there that run without hacks, but there are nice bonuses to cracking it, like being able to turn the clock speed up (removes slow downs from Megaman Powered Up and Final Fantasy Tactics:War of the Lions for example) and other little goodies like plugins. And ISOs of games that you totally own. (The only way to play Rockband and Kingdom Hearts, among others, on the PSPgo.)

Once you've hacked it, press select at the XMB to access a menu with all kinds of neat stuff:

You can use to adjust the clock speed to remove slowdown from games, or turn it down to save battery on the XMB, but be careful because you can make it sluggish or act funky by setting it wrong. I use 333 in game and [default] for the XMB personally.

You can also delve into the recovery menu, but be careful. Its unlikely that you'd do enough damage that you can't wipe it and restart from scratch, but I can't take responsibility if you do.

The one thing you want to do is if you have a PSPgo, then make sure that Configuration>Prevent Hibernation Delete is enabled. This gives you a reloadable save state for PSP games using the built in suspend feature.

You can also check out the registry hacks to enable WMA and Flash playback and delete you hibernation file manually. You can also switch the X/O buttons like on a Japanese PSP, but its use varies game to game, so I leave it disabled.

Step Two: Getting your Emulators

Emulators are here. (GBATemp's Big List of Emulators)

Wololo also has an easier to navigate list here (If you're overwhelmed by GBAtemp's)

Just drop in your GAME folder at PSP/GAME. Most of them have ROM folders within the game folder, and its pretty obvious which folder they go in. Some emulators have a file browser that dumps you in the root of your filesystem; in that case, just navigate to the folder you put your games, and most emulators will save that location for future use.

Now, emulation on PSP is nowhere near perfect; some games have serious or game breaking problems. Off the top of my head: Donkey Country series (SNES) does not work on SNES9xTYL, SuperFX games are unlikely to work, and Kingdom Hearts: Chain of Memories (GBA) crashes on the opening cinematic. N64 is pretty much a no go, I think only Super Mario 64 and a few others work.

PS1 works well with the PSP's built in emulator POPS, but don't ask me how to convert the isos, I never could figure it out. The site I download from has pre-converted PSX2PSP isos, so I just get those. They go in the PSP/GAME folder like your emulators, not in your ISOs folder (Discussed below).

Step Three: Other Hacking Stuff (You can ignore this section if your just after emulators)

ISOs: You can get PSP isos and csos and load them into /ISO/ and they'll appear in the XMB the same way that PSN games do. Can't help you find them, but if you use my hinted at search term above, you'll find them yourself. Google is your friend. There are also ways to rip them yourself, but I have no idea how, I have the PSPgo (no disc drive).

Plugins: I found this in 5 minutes of searching. QuickJump is a solid site, I've downloaded stuff from there for years.

Most have install instructions in readmes in each indivdual zip, and most of them have a /sepplugins/ that you can just dump in the root of your memory card, although be careful about overwriting your game.txt, POPS.txt, and vsh.txt files. If you want to use more than one plugin, you'll have to manually edit them for each plugin.

Example:

ms0:/seplugins/getinfo.prx 1

This is for the 'get info' plugin in the above plugin pack, just add a line for each plugin. The plugins listed in game.txt will activate in game, the ones in vsh.txt will activate on the XMB, and the ones in POPS.txt will activate in PSone classics. Refer to the included readme file or included .txt files for which ones to add it to. If you have a PSPgo and put the plugin on the internal memory, replace ms0 with ef0.

You can toggle plugins from the XMB's Select menu.

PSP Model Comparisons

PSP 1000

I would avoid this one unless you get a good deal on it. No commercial games ever used the expanded RAM of future models, but some homebrew does, so this is incapable of running some emulators and homebrew. The only advantages to the 1000 are that you can perma install CFW (along with some 2000 models), and the never used IR port that one homebrew uses (I remember seeing a TV remote app a long time ago). It also lacks the A/V Component out that future generations had, meaning no TV gaming. (Not a huge loss, but its pretty cool nonetheless.)

Still, it had a good build quality, some people swear by it. If you do get one, check and make sure what you intend to run will run on 1000 models.

PSP 2000/3000 (PSP Slim)

This is where it starts to get murky. The only difference between the 2000 and 3000 models are the screen (and no one agrees which is actually better) and some 2000 have an old board that CFW can be permanently installed to. The latter difference is irrelevant since it takes almost no time to recover your CFW on reboot, and most people don't cut their PSPs all the way off that often anyway, so if you can, look at the screen before you buy to see which you prefer. There are plugins that simulate a 3000 screen on the 1000/2000 by adjusting the contrast.

Other wise, there is no difference, and these are the models to get if you're after a PSP classic. If you get a PSP classic, check out the microSD adapters that can be found on eBay, they're cheaper than an actual memory stick, and take 2 microSDs for potentially more storage. (I remember when the 1GB memory stick cost $50, now you can 16-32 for less than $30.)

PSPgo

Some People hate it, some like me love it.

Pros:

  • Slimmer and easier to carry around with you
  • 16GB internal storage
  • Suspend States (that can act as full savestates with CFW, but only one at a time)
  • Bluetooth
  • Can connect a DS3 through Bluetooth and have a full controller (must have a PS3 to do this).
  • Combine that with a dock and A/V out cables, you have a mini game system that can also be taken on the go.

Cons:

  • No Disc Drive (This is the biggest, it means no cheap used games or some games being completely unavailable legally.)
  • Lack of accessory compatibility, some things like the camera don't work (apparently there is an adapter for them, but its imported and expensive.)
  • Accessories use the same port as the charging port (you have to get a dock and different powercable if you want A/V out and power at the same time.)
  • Uses its own unique accessory set and charging cable, and they're somewhat more expensive than their PSP classic counterparts.
  • Memory cards are more expensive, especially considering the 2xmicroSD adapters that you can get online now for the PSP classics.
